item.title: The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026
item.description:
Flipping through the highlights in and around Pinball Expo 2026.

It’s October in the Midwest, which means it’s time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago’s last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what’s new in the silver-ball universe.

Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball’s headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations fromJawsto the brand-newFallout. Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois.

As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball’s HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company’s 40-year history. After a stop at Gary’s podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, “at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest.”

While the industry may be expanding toward something more reminiscent of its glory days, there’s no doubt who still rules the market. With a steady stream of new license releases, Stern has cemented itself asthebrand in modern pinball.

What I saw on the expo floor, though, showed me that the remaining 10 percent of the market is doing some really interesting things, and hobbyist projects are booming. From modular home setups to open development kits that let anyone with silver-ball dreams try their hand at game design, there was something for everyone. In short, it’s a very exciting time to be a pinball fan.

Stern’s latest offering,Fallout, stood near the entrance of a convention floor packed with the latest machines from manufacturers like Jersey Jack, Barrels of Fun, Spooky Pinball, and others. I’ve attended this show for the last four years, and each year seems to bring new companies into the fold. Despite more than 25 years of advances in home entertainment, nothing quite matches the tactile thrill of launching a metal ball around a wooden cabinet.

Several companies showed off their latest attempts to bring pinball into virtual reality without abandoning physical controls, letting players wear a VR helmet while pressing real buttons on a pedestal setup. It’s a fun novelty that demonstrates what’s possible, but if the lines at the expo were any indication, most people still prefer walking up to a physical machine and enjoying the tactile controls, visuals, and sounds that come with it.

One of the biggest questions facing anyone buying a pinball machine for home use is what to do when you get bored with a $10,000 game. Until recently, the options were to sell it, find someone willing to trade, or build your own virtual pin setup with screens instead of physical playfields. The Multimorphic P3 team saw an opportunity for another approach.

According to Multimorphic co-creative director Stephen Silver, “The way the P3 is designed is that the lower two-thirds is a ball-tracking interactive display… We have floating mechanisms above the screen, floating flippers, floating slings, floating targets. And the upper third is a swappable play field. We’ve got 10 different play fields now that we can swap and change the entire game.”

As demonstrated by the much-hypedDungeon Crawler Carlprototype (whose lines never seemed to get shorter), the P3 system uses a playfield screen that can react to ball movement in real time, and the game can change to match player choices. InDungeon Crawler Carl, for instance, the display layout changes based on which book in the series the player chooses.

“We’re planning on doing seven books in the game… you can play them in any order you want,” Silver explained. ” The idea being that you get to Faction Wars—the events of the seventh book—it’s a perfectwizard mode. When we started this,Faction Warswas the last book in the series. It still feel(s) like a good wrapping-up point for this story that we’re telling. In the future, we could always be open to adding more books, but right now that’s the plan.”

The first two entries in the book series had playable pin versions on the show floor, and Silver says that “every single book itself is the equivalent depth of a ’90s Williams game… It’s like seven really solid games in one,” Silver said.

Dungeon Crawler Carlwill enter production “at the end of the year, and then it should be rolling out to delivery early next year,” he said.

The platform’s versatility extends beyond in-house designs. Multimorphic offers a free software development kit (SDK) that lets community members design and distribute their own table creations for the P3 system. Machine owners can swap physical overlay kits or remove them entirely to play original games on the reactive screen.

“There are 30 different games available on the system now because you can do software-only games,” Silver said. “It’s the only third-party development platform in pinball. So anybody can download the free SDK and develop third-party software games… and release it through our store to an audience of P3 owners that are hungry for new content.”

Sitting on one of the more unassuming tables of the PinExpo show floor wasPocket Pinball, a free Android APK that lets users load anyVisual Pinball X(VPX) table on their phone or tablet. But the project’s developer, Johnny Zen, had something else to show off: a closed beta for his Pinball Construction Set. An homage to the1982 classic Bill Budge Apple II gameof the same name, the browser-based tool lets users design their own pinball machine with an easy drag-and-drop interface. Multimorphic may have the only free pinball SDK for now, but if Zen has his way, that won’t be true for long.

Whereas most modern pinball designs start at the CAD desk, the upcoming Pinball Construction Set keeps the process entirely within a browser. Zen compares the system to building a coaster inRoller Coaster Tycoon: Users can choose between three styles or start with a blank slate. After selecting a template, such as a standard or wide-body layout, they can add traditional design elements like ramps, targets, and scoops by clicking and dragging them into place.

The program is still in closed beta, but aspiring pinball developerscan register their interestto be notified when it becomes publicly available. Zen also plans to add a marketplace where users can commission artwork from freelance artists. “If you needed some artwork for your apron or playfield, you basically look at the artist profiles, then the app will send the artist’s team the exact measurements of what you need,” he said.

One of the most exciting trends in pinball’s modern resurgence is the rise of homebrew design, with passionate hobbyists turning basement-built machines into careers with some of the industry’s biggest players. Often serving as playable resumes, homebrew games give aspiring designers a chance to flex their creative muscles without the licensing restrictions that come with producing commercial machines.

One of this year’s homebrew highlights wasShaolin Flow,an ode to the great Hong Kong action movies that those of us who grew up in the ’90s watched on Saturday afternoon network TV. Complete with an optional Wu-Tang soundtrack,Shaolin Flowlets players choose between traditional flipper-button controls and a more punchy approach. Two fist-shaped sensors sit atop the playfield, to the left and right of the flippers. Players activate the flippers by throwing punches over the sensor.

What initially looked like a gimmick quickly proved to be a great time. Adding a physical element to an already physical game felt more natural than I expected, and the absence of any perceptible input lag made the experience seamless.

As the tools for designing and building pinball machines become more accessible, the homebrew scene continues to grow. Each year brings more entries to the floor, transforming what was once a smaller corner of proudly displayed projects into a dedicated, walled-off section featuring games from the future stars of pinball design. This year’s homebrew showstopper could see its creator designing a licensed table for one of the industry’s major manufacturers by the following year’s show.

Pinball Expo isn’t just an industry trade event; it’s also a celebration of every era of pinball history. Volunteers haul machines from their personal collections to the show floor, where the general public can play them all weekend. And it’s not just balls and flippers. Walk the aisles, and you’ll see artists, merch and crafts vendors, accessories, retro video games, traditional arcades, and enough aftermarket mod kits to turn any pinball machine into a second hobby.

For decades, pinball production was concentrated among a handful of major manufacturers in the Chicagoland area. While the region might still be the industry’s epicenter, newer challengers to Stern’s dominance, like Texas-basedBarrels of Funor European producers likeDutch Pinball, show that things are changing.

Today, aspiring developers can turn a good idea into a playable VPX table without ever putting down their phone. Whether it’s a bedroom developer working with a free SDK or one of the industry’s biggest players, pinball is being made by more people in more places, and fans are all the better for it.

item.title: Review: Carrie is a triumphant remix with one major flaw
item.description:
Mike Flanagan’s re-imagining of Stephen King’s classic is well worth watching.

Carrie White, the telekinetic prom queen from hell, is one of the most beloved horror icons in popular culture. First introduced in Stephen King’s 1974 novel,Carrie, the character was immortalized in director Brian De Palma’s 1976 adaptation, widely regarded as one of the best horror films of all time. It’s certainly one of the best King adaptations. So Mike Flanagan faced a massive challenge when he signed on to create an eight-episode miniseries for Prime Video based on the book, released just in time to mark the 50th anniversary of de Palma’s film.

I was among the skeptics who questioned why aCarrieminiseries was even necessary, although as a diehard Flanagan fan (“Flana-fan”?), I was willing to give him the benefit of the doubt. If anyone has an affinity for smartly adapting horror in general, and King’s work in particular, it’s Flanagan. And you know what? With one (very big) exception, Flanagan pulls it off, giving us a richly textured version of the story that is as much about kindness and lost innocence as bloody, vengeful rage—although we get plenty of the latter, too.

(Many spoilers below forthe noveland the1976 film, but there are no major reveals for the new series until after the second gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

King initially meant to write a short story after reading an article in Life magazine about telekinesis. He imagined a scene where a bullied young girl gets her first period in a high school locker room as the centerpiece of the story but struggled to capture how his female character would react in that situation. He wrote three pages and tossed them in the trash. Fortunately, his wife Tabitha salvaged the pages and convinced King to try again. He eventually expanded it into a full-length novel, basing Carrie on two girls he knew in high school who had been bullied relentlessly.

Fun fact: In an early draft of the infamous prom scene, King had Carrie grow horns and use her telekinetic powers to take out an airplane flying overhead. His editor convinced him to go with a more “subtle” ending. Granted, dumping pig’s blood on his protagonist and having her destroy the entire town in revenge is hardly subtle, but it’s a vast improvement on devil horns.

Carriewas not an instant bestseller; it was the mass-market paperback edition that sold over a million copies and put King on the map as a writer. It also piqued the interest of director Brian De Palma after a mutual friend of King’s recommended the book. De Palma instantly recognized the film potential and optioned the rights before searching for the perfect actress to play Carrie.

Sissy Spacek was still relatively unknown, although she’d had a breakthrough role in the 1973 neo-noir dramaBadlands. Her husband, a production designer, convinced her to audition for the film. She wasn’t de Palma’s first choice for Carrie, but Spacek was determined to win him over, even rubbing Vaseline in her hair and wearing her seventh grade sailor dress to the audition. She got the part, and the rest is cinematic history.

De Palma kept most of the novel’s key scenes intact in his adaptation, with a few changes. For instance, in the book, Carrie kills her mother, after the latter stabs her, by telekinetically stopping her heart, calling it a “gift” since Margaret White has always longed for “darkness.” In the film, Carrie impales Margaret (Piper Laurie) with flying kitchen knives, crucified within a door frame, before perishing herself. The director also tried to include a framing device in which stones fall from the sky onto the White family home—a key moment from Carrie’s childhood in the book—but in the opening scene the rocks just looked like falling raindrops, and there was a mechanical malfunction while filming the house’s final destruction by falling stones. So De Palma opted to destroy it by fire instead.

In the novel, survivor Sue Snell is psychically drawn to a dying Carrie, experiencing the tormented girl’s final moments in a kind of mind meld as she comforts her. De Palma opted to endCarriewith one of the best jump scares in film. A repentant Sue (Amy Irving) visits Carrie’s grave with flowers, only to have a hand shoot from under the soil and grab her arm; Sue wakes up screaming from her nightmare, still traumatized by the events on prom night. De Palma shot the scene backward to make it feel like a dreamscape. And that was actually Spacek’s hand bursting up through the soil; she let herself be buried on set to pull it off.

Carriewas a critical and box office hit, snagging Oscar nominations for Spacek and Laurie—a rare thing for a horror film. And the film has withstood the test of time, as compulsively watchable 50 years later as it was in 1976. The tragic story of an emotionally damaged, tormented girl with supernatural gifts, pushed to her breaking point, seems to resonate with something psychologically primal in all of us. Others have tried and failed to recapture that magic. The less said about the1999 sequel, the2002 TV film, the2013 remake, and the 1988Broadway musical, the better.

Enter Flanagan, who boldly set out to reinventCarriefor the 21st century. The showrunner has a gift for creatively remixing classic material in interesting ways, while remaining true to the spirit of the original. Another strength is his ability to build memorable, multifaceted characters, and he has eight episodes, not two hours, to do so. Flanagan reclaims certain elements, such as the stones raining down on the Whites’ house. The novel was also partly epistolary, including segments of fictional court transcripts and news coverage created by King (who enjoyed mimicking different writing styles). Flanagan incorporates video interviews as a framing device, in which surviving witnesses recount their memories of the tragic events.

But there are also significant changes. Carrie in King’s novel and De Palma’s film is a flinching, socially inept, mousey misfit. She lost her father as a baby and has been bullied all her life, not to mention being physically and emotionally abused at home by her religious zealot mother. In Flanagan’s version, Carrie (Summer H. Howell) has been homeschooled since birth. The death of her conspiracy theorist father (Tahmoh Penikett) in a freak construction accident forces Carrie and her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), into the real world after years of hardly ever leaving the house. (A social worker describes the family as having been a “cult of three.”)

This Carrie is smart, two grades ahead in terms of academic achievement, surprisingly open and curious, and an avid reader—thanks to the kindness of a next-door neighbor who would regularly leave books for Carrie to read on the sly by hiding them in a shared birdhouse. None of her fellow students catch her frequent literary allusions, but the principal, Henry Grayle (Matthew Lillard), does. So does Peter Morton (Tom Bagley), the gay guidance counselor. He and Carrie exchange a few of their favorite book quotes, after which he shows her the wonders of the high school library (“It’s all for you”).

But Flanagan’s Carrie is also extremely sheltered and unprepared for the harsh realities of high school in the 21st century, in addition to grieving for her father. First her gold cross sets off the metal detector. Then she thinks the school shooting drill is for real and has a panic attack. She’s never played volleyball or any team sport, so gym class is a disaster.

And then comes the infamous locker room scene and Carrie’s first period. De Palma’s camera lingered just a bit too longingly on the naked adolescent girls in the showers, although the scene did capture Carrie’s extreme vulnerability in that moment. Flanagan’s version has Carrie start her period fully clothed—but wearing white pants. High school bully Chris (Alison Thornton) pushes her into the shower before leading the other girls in a chant of “plug it up” while pelting her with sanitary napkins and tampons. And of course it’s all captured on multiple cell phones.

The 22-year-old Howell,best knownto date for playing Alison Pierce in the Chucky franchise, beat out 1,400 young actresses to play Carrie. She didn’t even read King’s novel or watch the 1976 movie, so she could interpret Flanagan’s take on the character. Spacek defined the role, but Howell redefines it with just as much assurance. She hits every single note, registers every small shift in expression and emotion, in a stellar performance that should cement her status as a gifted young actress on the rise.

WARNING: Major spoilers for the Mike Flanagan series below. Stop reading now if you haven’t finished watching.)

Lillard brings a jaded weariness to Principal Grayle—a once-idealistic educator whose kindness has been beaten into submission. But he still shows some fire when Chris’ high-powered lawyer father, John (Michael Trucco), threatens to sue the school, reminding John (in a moment lifted from the novel) that, by his reasoning, the school could counter-sue and that Chris’ long history of bullying would be laid open during discovery.

In the De Palma film, John Travolta’s Billy was a dim-witted jock, bonded to Nancy Allen’s vapid Chris by hormonal lust and their shared nasty, brutish natures. Neither had any redeeming qualities. That’s not the case in Flanagan’s series. Arthur Conti’s Billy is a high school dropout who works on a farm when not dealing drugs to partying high schoolers. He’s dark and broody, smart and sarcastic, a compulsive rule-breaker. And he’s dangerous—catnip for a spoiled, rebellious golden girl like Chris, whose perfect life has unexpectedly hit the skids. Her parents are divorcing, the father she idolizes is facing financial ruin, and since she didn’t apply for financial aid in time, she can’t join her bestie, Sue (Siena Agudong), at Duke University in the fall.

None of this excuses Chris’ malicious behavior, not just toward Carrie but toward her future stepsister, Brooklyn (Rowan Danielle), and the school as a whole, mostly via a fake Instagram account devoted to smearing students and faculty alike. It’s Carrie who asks the key question: Why go to such great lengths to target Carrie particularly? Chris’ answer—“I don’t know. You were weird, and you pissed me off”—speaks to her profound lack of self-awareness. Yet her recklessness and stubborn pride seal her doom. Chris is given many chances to reverse course, face accountability, and do the right thing; however torn, she can never bring herself to do it until it is much too late.

Flanagan improves on both De Palma’s film and King’s novel in his treatment of faith, embodied in Carrie’s mother, Margaret White. Margaret is a cartoonish caricature in those earlier incarnations, with her candles and crucifixes, sexual repression, and psychotic rants about sin and atonement. Flanagan understands the complicated nature of faith; he created the exquisiteMidnight Mass, after all, which also starred Sloyan (part of the “Flana-fam” of actors) in a pivotal role.

Sloyan was the perfect choice to play Margaret. She’s a grieving widow who has spent the last 15 years shutting out the world out of fear, ill-equipped to hold down even a job as a checkout clerk. She can’t help judging customers for, say, buying vibrators and condoms and helpfully lecturing them on their poor life choices. She’s intelligent, like Carrie, and has clearly done an excellent job homeschooling her daughter. However nutty her specific beliefs might be, she is not always wrong in her assessments; she’s just so rigidly unlikable, nobody wants to cede her the points.

Where King’s Margaret actively disliked her daughter—viewing her as the polluted spawn of the night her drunken husband effectively raped her—Sloyan’s Margaret clearly loves Carrie, wanting only to protect her from a world of sin and depravity. (She also clearly loved and depended upon her late husband.) She wages battle on behalf of her bullied daughter with admirable ferocity. Flanagan understands another crucial aspect of Margaret’s faith: it’s all about control. So when Margaret feels that control slipping away—when she’s forced to work and confront the ugliness of the world or when Carrie pushes back on her authority—she throws herself into re-exerting her control, even if that means locking Carrie in the prayer closet for hours on end to save her immortal soul.

Above all, Flanagan understands how even a mother’s love can be poisoned by fear when Carrie uses her newfound powers to wrest control of the household from her mother. The final interaction between mother and daughter starts with Margaret washing away all the blood in the bath, recalling how she did the same thing the night Carrie was born. As they prepare to pray together, Carrie asks if god can forgive her for what she has done. “Even if god doesn’t, I forgive you,” Margaret replies, before tearfully asking if Carrie can forgive her—for what we know (but Carrie doesn’t) will be Margaret’s attempted murder of her own child

King’s novel alludes to Margaret’s grandmother having similar telekinetic abilities, which Margaret had always attributed to witchcraft, and the novel ends with an Appalachian woman writing a letter to her sister in 1988, telling her about her 4-year-old daughter’s emerging telekinetic gifts. He even hints at a recessive “TK” gene as the cause. Flanagan turned all that into a cult of women with supernatural gifts, led by Adelaide (Kate Siegel), who sense Carrie’s nascent power and track her down. (Here it is Adelaide, not Carrie, who stops Margaret’s heart after interviewing her as a witness.) He also introduces Emmaline (Thalia Dudek), who befriends Carrie and encourages her worst instincts, only to be revealed as an astral projection of the real Emmaline. (She is definitely not a high school student.)

Of course, everything comes down to that famous prom scene, with Carrie being crowned queen before being doused with pig’s blood. De Palma’s sequence followed that moment with an eerie silence, the only sound that of the clanking empty bucket, before all hell breaks loose. Flanagan chooses to have Carrie telekinetically explode everyone’s cell phone and have the screen cut to black as we hear agonized screams to close the penultimate episode. Yet the final episode opens with another interview segment; those segments keep interrupting the action, which is a bit frustrating but forgivable. (There are alreadyfan cutspopping up on YouTube stitching together the prom night footage without the breaks.)

There is really only one flaw in Flanagan’sCarrie,and it’s a major change from the source material: Carrie is not solely responsible for the prom night carnage—and she survives (a twist that also featured in the 2002 TV film). Sue admits she knew Carrie was “fucked” on the very first day because she was genuinely kind and innocent, admirable qualities that make certain people like Chris feel inferior and lash out with cruelty. But plenty of others found Carrie disarmingly likable. We see glimpses of a darker Carrie—telekinetically breaking Chris’ nose in class, for instance, and telling her to “plug it up” as she walks past. Honestly, Chris deserved it. But Carrie only feels shame and guilt over her actions, rejecting Emmaline’s celebratory gloating over the incident.

Is this a person so psychologically damaged that she would quickly turn murderous and take out an entire town in revenge for a vicious prank? Flanagan doesn’t seem to think so, since he blinks and lets Emmaline “take the wheel” after poor Tommy (Joel Oulette) is killed when Carrie brings down an overhead walkway. Emmaline (whoisthat damaged) temporarily possesses Carrie to inflict the worst of the ensuing deadly havoc on her behalf. That one creative decision takes away Carrie’s agency at the most crucial moment and seriously undercuts the foundation on which the whole character arc rests.

Of course, Carrie does plenty of damage on her own, including crushing Billy and Chris to death after flipping their car when Billy tries to run her down. She’s both horrified and strangely elated by what she’s done. But she just feels horror when Emmaline vanishes abruptly, and Carrie realizes what she’s done to the town, limping home for the final confrontation with her murder-minded mother. That’s the devastating revelation that truly breaks her: She’s a monster in the eyes of her own mother.

Somehow that one huge misstep isn’t enough to sink this compelling series—a tribute to the power of the core story.

As for why Carrie survives, Flanagan has plans for another two seasons, taking us into uncharted territory with King’s blessing. Prom night set Carrie down a dark path, drunk on her newfound power, with a weakened moral compass. She’s unwittingly caught between two different factions seeking to exploit her immense power—her new bestie, Emmaline, and Adelaide’s group—plus another group that seems intent on killing Carrie and others like her. It will be interesting to see what Flanagan comes up with, given the chance, now that he’s freed from the constraints of the original novel.

All eight episodes ofCarrieare now streaming on Prime Video, as is the 1976 film.

item.title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
item.description:
OpenEvidence is booming despite questions about accuracy and ads.

Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.

Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.

The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.

OpenEvidence has won praise from medical professionals who have found it helped ease workloads, according to interviews with eight senior physicians.

But it faces a nascent threat from large AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, who are making a push into the space. Its growing influence has also prompted scrutiny from researchers concerned over the accuracy of its results, as doctors grow more dependent on an AI tool shaping the course of treatments.

The company’s rapid ascent has attracted nearly $1 billion in investment in the past 18 months, from backers including Andreessen Horowitz, Blackstone, Thrive Capital, and Sequoia. The group raised $250 million in its latest funding round in September at a $15 billion valuation.

OpenEvidence booked $100 million in “ad buys”—a metric that covers current and future advertising commitments—for this year at the end of 2025, according to a person close to the company. The startup is on track to generate between $400 million and $500 million through ads by the end of 2026, the person added.

Nadler’s company has penetrated an established market for medical software that was sluggish to incorporate generative AI models. Dutch IT group Wolters Kluwer released an AI version of its leading subscription-based UpToDate medical software tool in October 2025, nearly two years after OpenEvidence entered the market.

Central to OpenEvidence’s pitch is a focused source list consisting of peer-reviewed journals such as the New England Journal of Medicine and the Journal of the American Medical Association.

“OpenEvidence allows me to provide a lot of context about my patient, find information, and make decisions faster,” said Nina Singh, a medical resident at the University of California San Francisco. “It’s a really useful tool.”

Widespread appeal has helped OpenEvidence forge relationships with several hospitals and specialist clinics such as Mount Sinai Health System and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, embedding its tool within the organizations’ electronic health records.

Paul Testa, chief health informatics officer at NYU Langone, said that the hospital system sought a formal tie-up with OpenEvidence after it found clinicians were already using the tool as an “independent resource.”

“We chose to deeply integrate a clinically informed version of OpenEvidence into the care process to ensure two things: first, our clinicians can get the most from these AI tools, and second, they use them securely,” he said.

OpenEvidence has leveraged its popularity with doctors to slowly expand into other domains, including ambient documentation—note-taking during doctors’ patient interactions.

Critics have questioned whether the company’s ad-based model warrants its high valuation, while its decision to withdraw from the EU and UK earlier this year over the bloc’s AI Act has stymied its expansion into two key markets.

Mike Vernal, a partner at venture firm Conviction and an OpenEvidence investor, said that the company’s popularity among physicians represented its strongest defense against startup rivals and incumbents.

Nadler said it will also launch clinical trials in the coming weeks, partnering with researchers to target cancer and rare diseases. It plans to apply AI models to drug discovery and draw on pre-existing literature to generate novel scientific hypotheses.

“The end game is literature-based drug discovery,” Nadler said, referencing the field of data mining scientific literature for insights. “The economic value of that as a company is going to dwarf by orders of magnitude whatever we could have charged hospitals or advertisers.”

Alexander Tarashansky, the creator of Claude Science, an Anthropic platform that supports research scientists, has also joined the company to support its clinical work.

The company needs to see off competition from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI, which has also made a play for the space with ChatGPT for healthcare. Anthropic has also released healthcare tools, though it recently partnered with OpenEvidence to bring the tools to 100 low- and middle-income countries.

“The fact that doctors are adopting and using a piece of software of their own volition means there is a degree of differentiation that OpenEvidence can really lean on,” said Nworah Ayogu, a partner at investor Thrive Capital.

But analysis of OpenEvidence’s effectiveness has led to mixed results.

One study by the Mayo Clinic, an investor in the startup, found that it “provided accurate, evidence-based recommendations” in all five patient case studies that were sampled, although its impact on treatment decisions was more limited.

Other research, including a June paper published in Nature, found that it underperformed general-purpose AI models such as Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s GPT on clinical benchmarks.

Eric Oermann, a neurosurgeon at NYU Langone, said there was a lack of research into the performance of individual AI tools and scant guidance on how to implement the tools in a clinical setting.

There are also widely held concerns that more junior doctors could fall foul by relying too heavily on OpenEvidence and other systems without first mastering basic knowledge of particular conditions and their prescribed treatment options.

“It’s a fun, friendly competitive pressure to play with benchmarks… [But] there’s no question of what AI tool physicians trust and use,” Nadler said.

Additional reporting by George Hammond in San Francisco.

item.title: SpaceX to attempt Starship catch on next flight, with eye on rapid cadence increase
item.description:
“We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA.”

In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground.

Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company’s long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the “Starmind” data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket.

That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company’s president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle.

It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test, Musk said, to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight.

Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight.

One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico.

“We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” Shotwell said.

As for what comes after this test flight, Shotwell said SpaceX would attempt to refly a Starship upper stage “early” next year. The company will also seek to complete a long-delayed refueling test of Starship early in 2027. This Starship-to-Starship refueling demonstration is an important milestone for SpaceX and NASA to prove the viability of Starship being refueled in low-Earth orbit for lunar missions.

Refueling on this scale has never been done before, and the company needs to get data on the efficiency of such transfers and the rate of boil-off of liquid oxygen and methane in space. This data will refine projections for how many launches are needed to support a Starship landing on the Moon for NASA as part of the Artemis Program.

For SpaceX, the near-term priority is reaching a high flight cadence for Starship and pushing the boundaries of vehicle reuse to enable it.

Musk, who often offers hyper-optimistic timeframes, said he expects Starship to reach a “weekly” flight cadence during the first half of 2027 and to launch twice weekly during the second half of the year. The key will be how much Starship can be reused.

“The rate at which we launch Starship will increase dramatically as we solve rapid and complete reusability,” Musk said. “At first there will be a little bit of refurbishment that’s needed between each flight, and we’ll iron out the need for any refurbishment such that you can immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.”

That’s the vision, at least. Achieving complete reusability with an orbital rocket has never been done before, so SpaceX’s engineering team will undoubtedly face some significant hurdles. Over time, however, they are likely to get close to the vision of launching, landing, and reflying rockets.

SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads in 2027 with the Starship rocket. Shotwell said the company would continue launching Starlink V3 satellites, the second generation of “mobile” satellites that deliver direct-to-cell connectivity, as well as Starmind data center prototypes, next year. During the earnings call, neither Musk nor Shotwell addressed, nor were asked by financial analysts, about thecontroversial throttling of Starlink capabilitiesfor Ukraine in its war with Russia.
